newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel won't rule out tax hike for 98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Waigel won't rule out tax hike for 98 budget.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under intense pressure to plug holes in the state finances, insisted on Saturday he would not rule out raising taxes as a last resort to help fund public spending in 1998.
While privatisation would take precedence in the search for additional revenues, other possibilities including tax increases could not be excluded, Waigel said.

But tax hikes were "a last and undesirable resort," Waigel told reporters in Nuremberg where he was attending a meeting of so-called Sudeten Germans expelled from then-Czechoslovakia after the Second World War.
With unemployment forcing the government to spend an additional 20 billion marks on jobless benefits per year such a move could not be completely ignored, he said.

Waigel also appealed to the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in the ruling coalition, to relax their firm opposition to tax hikes which may be the only way to arrive at a budget that meets the demands of the Federal Constitution.

"The FDP not only shares responsibility for taxes, it must also accept responsibility for drafting a budget which is in line with the Constitution," Waigel was quoted as telling Bild am Sonntag in an interview.
The Constitution states that a government's net new borrowing must not exceed the amount it spends on investment.
Waigel said a decision on whether to raise taxes will be taken at the end of June. Bild am Sonntag released a copy of the interview ahead of publication on Sunday.
He was speaking after a week which saw Bonn scrambling to reduce its budget deficit for 1997 in the face of a steep shortfall in tax revenues.

Under a controversial plan announced on Thursday, Waigel is seeking to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves to reduce the public deficit and debt in a bid to qualify Germany for monetary union.
An official estimate said tax revenue in 1997 will be 18 billion marks less than expected, casting further doubt on whether Germany can meet the Maastricht Treaty's convergence criteria.

Separately, FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhardt said his party would only be able to support a 1998 budget which did not raise taxes. The coalition had already agreed not to raise taxes for the 1997 budget, Gerhardt told n-tv television in an interview.
Hans-Peter Repnik, deputy parliamentary leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), said he could barely imagine Germany would be able to avoid tax increases in 1998.

Repnik told Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper the coalition was considering bringing forward by one year a rise in indirect taxes -- petrol tax or value-added-tax -- that had originally been planned to help fund a reform of the pensions system in 1999.
